title: Acheria the Fox
subtitle: A fox recruits a wolf to distract a shepherd

learningObjectives.text: What does Acheria the fox do?
What kind of trickster is he?

fox.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
fox.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
fox.locator: ACHERIA, THE FOX.; ACHERIA, THE FOX., normalized characters 18-1329
fox.excerpt: One day a fox was hungry. He did not know what to think. He saw a shepherd pass every day with his flock, and he said to himself that he ought to steal his milk and his cheese, and to have a good feast; but he needed some one to help him in order to effect anything. So he goes off to find a wolf, and he says to him, "Wolf, wolf! we ought to have a feast with such a shepherd's milk and cheese. You, you shall go to where the flocks are feeding, and from a distance you must howl, 'Uhur, uhur, uhur.' The man, after having milked his sheep, drives them into the field, with his dog, very early in the morning, and he stops at home to do his work, and then he makes his cheese; and, when you have begun to howl 'Uhur, uhur,' and the dog to bark, the shepherd will leave everything else, and will go off full speed. During this time I will steal the milk, and we will share it when you come to me." The wolf agreed to have a feast, and set out. He did just what the fox had told him. The dog began to bark when the wolf approached. And when the man heard that he went off, leaving everything, and our fox goes and steals the vessel in which the curdled milk was. What does he do then, before the arrival of the wolf? He gently, gently takes off the cream, thinly, thinly, and he eats all the contents of the jug.
fox.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: The fox of the Pyrenees
narrativeBlocks.body: Acheria — 'the fox' in the Basque tales — is the Labourd tradition's own trickster: small, clever, and always hungry, playing the same games Reynard plays in France.

narrativeBlocks.title: The played-dead trick
narrativeBlocks.body: His signature move: he lies in the road pretending to be dead — and when a cart of fish comes past, the driver tosses 'the dead fox' on the cart for the skin. Acheria sits up, gorges, throws the rest off, and runs.

narrativeBlocks.title: The trick on the wolf
narrativeBlocks.body: He leads bigger animals into traps with promises — the wolf ends up with his tail frozen in the pond after 'fishing' through the ice all night, while Acheria is already gone with the meal.

narrativeBlocks.title: A trickster who wins and loses
narrativeBlocks.body: Acheria isn't invincible — some Labourd tales end with the fox out-foxed. The trickster's lesson runs both ways: cunning wins, until it doesn't.

narrativeBlocks.title: A cousin of Anansi and Coyote
narrativeBlocks.body: Every tradition keeps its small-clever-animals: Basque Acheria belongs to the same world-family as the spider of the Gold Coast and the rabbits and coyotes we'll meet later.
